Living Well / Free resources

Meaning, wonder & spiritual curiosity

A useful way in

Choose one place to begin.

A conversation or a reflective question can be a useful beginning. Explore different approaches to meaning at your own pace.

Meaning is not only a subject to read about. It can also be a way of paying attention to a familiar activity, a person, or an unanswered question. These selections offer conversations, context, and reflective invitations rather than a single account of how life should be lived.

Start with: On Being: a conversation about attention. Open the Mary Oliver conversation and choose audio or the transcript. You can begin with a short passage.

On Being: a conversation about attention

The On Being Project

A way into meaning through a person and a conversation rather than a list of conclusions. The selected interview connects creative work with attention to the world.

Begin here: Open the Mary Oliver conversation and choose audio or the transcript. You can begin with a short passage.

Access: Free web audio and transcript; no subscription needed for this selection.

Religious traditions, with context

Harvard University, The Pluralism Project

Spiritual vocabulary means more when it is connected to the people and histories that use it. This collection helps provide that context.

Begin here: Read Rivers of Faith, then choose one tradition that you would like to understand better.

Access: Free public essays; no registration needed to read.

Perspective: Academic religious context

Context & source

A landscape of consciousness

Closer To Truth

For a larger question after an ordinary one: how does felt experience relate to the world we can describe? This is an orientation to different proposed answers.

Begin here: Begin with Exploring Consciousness rather than trying to navigate the entire theory map.

Access: Free public introduction; no registration needed to read.

Grateful Living: practice space

A Network for Grateful Living

A collection of questions, poetry, and modest invitations to notice what matters in an ordinary day.

Keep the context

Take what is useful, thoughtfully.

Begin with a format you enjoy. A conversation lets you hear how someone arrives at a view; a contextual introduction helps explain unfamiliar language; a reflective question leaves room for your own response. Keep the experience of finding something meaningful separate from accepting every explanation offered for it.

Selections are based on public source review, not a claim that Nolan uses every resource or belongs to the organizations listed.
